newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's opposition rallies mix party and politics.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's opposition rallies mix party and politics.

text.p: "So, you've come to watch our revolution?" asked a smiling young woman in a quilted jacket, pausing for a moment from blowing an ear-splitting whistle.
Belgrade's main square and another close by have been alive with protest against Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic every day for a month.
Supporters of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition blow whistles, set off fireworks, play rock music and carry flickering candles in demonstrations in Belgrade and across Serbia.

Badges proclaiming "I Am A Marcher", colourful student posters and balloons are among the paraphernalia of protest, swiftly made and distributed after Milosevic overturned local election results in November.

In one torchlight procession, students waved torches and lanterns and some wore miners' lamps "to enlighten a city in political darkness". Belgraders switched the lights in their flats on and off to show support as marchers snaked by.
Some marchers play trumpets and drums, dress in costume, or simply join in with their toddlers and dogs. One march was led by a man dressed as a Halloween pumpkin.
The carnival atmosphere belies Zajedno's serious political demands, that Milosevic reinstate annulled local elections which threaten his ruling Socialists, the former communists.
Most marchers acknowledge their street protests are not about to topple the president but see the campaign as a prelude to challenging his rule in Serbian general elections next year.
The opposition bristled at one Western media report that its ranks included right-wing nationalists, insisting that theirs is a genuinely popular and democratic movement.
It took time for trade unionists to march because they believed their grievances on pay and workers' rights might be swept away by the opposition's political agenda. They also feared being sacked.
But now they are starting to join in.
Up to 250,000 people, about 10 percent of Belgrade's population, marched over the weekend. It was a record turnout.
"If someone can't make it they almost see it as their duty to get someone else, a friend or a relative, to go along," one march organiser said.
Police have made no effort to stop the marches, although memories linger of 1991, when Milosevic used tanks to crush Serbia's last significant street protests.

Zajedno leader Vuk Draskovic told Russian television: "The vast majority of police are on our side. All young officers who voted for the opposition are on our side because they have been robbed of election victory as well."

Marchers have come to Belgrade from towns outside the capital and a delegation from the southern industrialised city of Nis, where a court ordered the electoral commission to respect a Zajedno electoral victory, even got to see Milosevic.
The opposition want to use marches to spread their word outside Belgrade and counter the influence of the state media, which they say distorts their message.

Zoran Djindjic, another opposition leader, promised his movement would become a "world champion" of long-running protests and vowed to bring in 1,000 people from each of 30 separate towns to join a Belgrade rally in the New Year.
Each night he tells the crowd: "See you tomorrow, same time, same place."
